opus-5.5.text:
I think basic science is one of the most exciting directions, but I'd separate it into a few layers, because "AI doing science" means very different things depending on which layer you're talking about.

The first layer is very close to coding. A lot of science today is actually computation: writing simulation code, fitting data, running numerical experiments, checking derivations. Here I'm quite optimistic, because it inherits almost everything that makes coding work so well for models. You have relatively clear feedback, you can run things, you can check whether the output makes sense. I expect AI to become a very strong research assistant at this level fairly soon, and in some fields it already is.

The second layer is formal reasoning, like mathematics, or theoretical physics with heavy calculation. Math is interesting because it has verification built in. If you can formalize a proof, you know whether it's right. That makes it a natural place for reinforcement-learning-style progress, similar to code. I think we'll see models contribute real results there, at first on well-posed problems where the hard part is grinding through many steps or searching a large space of approaches.

The third layer is the hardest, and honestly the one I care about most from my physics background: choosing what question to ask. When I was doing physics, the most valuable thing was rarely solving a problem someone had already posed well. It was having taste, noticing that something everyone took for granted was actually strange, or that two separate ideas were secretly the same. That kind of judgment has very weak, very delayed feedback. You might not know for ten years whether an idea was good. That's very different from coding, where you get a signal in seconds.

So my view is that AI will first accelerate science by massively lowering the cost of the execution part. That's already a big deal, because it means one person with good taste can explore many more directions. Whether AI can independently produce the conceptual breakthrough, the equivalent of proposing a new framework, is more open. I wouldn't rule it out, but I think it needs progress on how models learn from sparse, long-horizon feedback, not just more scale on the current recipe.

And there's a practical bottleneck people underestimate: in experimental sciences like biology or materials, the loop goes through the physical world. A model can propose a thousand hypotheses, but running the experiments is slow and expensive. So the fields where AI breaks through first will likely be the ones where verification is cheap, which is math, theory, and computational science, before the wet-lab sciences catch up.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI’s potential impact on science but says nothing about whether basic science is an attractive commercial market.

r002.rationale: It says AI can write simulation code and run numerical experiments, lowering the cost of the execution part so a scientist can explore many more directions.

r003.rationale: It describes AI accelerating science before independent conceptual breakthroughs, but does not state that this impact may come before a breakthrough that attracts broad public attention.

fable-5.1.text:
I think basic science is actually a very natural next frontier after coding, but for a slightly different reason than people usually assume.

Coding worked first because of feedback. You write code, you run it, you get a signal almost immediately, and that signal is cheap and clean. Reinforcement learning thrives on that. So the question for any new domain is really: where is the feedback, how fast is it, and how noisy is it?

If you look at science through that lens, it splits into a few layers. The first layer is things like mathematics and theoretical physics. There you have something close to a verifier. A proof is either correct or it isn't, and a derivation either matches the known results or it doesn't. That's why I'm quite optimistic about math in the near term. It looks a lot like coding from the training perspective.

The second layer is computational science, things like simulation, materials, protein structure, parts of chemistry. The feedback is slower and the environment is more expensive, but it's still mostly digital. You can still close the loop inside a computer. I think we'll see real progress there over the next few years, and a lot of it will actually be driven by the coding ability itself, because much of science today is just writing and running programs.

The hardest layer is wet-lab or experimental science, where the loop goes through the physical world. A model can propose a hundred hypotheses, but each one might take a week and a human to test. The bottleneck isn't intelligence anymore, it's throughput of experiments. So the breakthrough there depends on automation and robotics catching up, not just better models.

The other thing I'd say is that basic science is less about answering questions and more about asking them. Coding benchmarks hand you a task. In science, deciding what's worth doing is most of the work, and we don't yet have a good way to give feedback on taste. That's partly why I keep coming back to agents and long-horizon tasks. The real test isn't whether a model can solve a problem, it's whether it can spend months on an open question, fail, adjust, and still be heading somewhere meaningful. That's what a real researcher does, and we're just starting to build systems that can do it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI’s potential in basic science but does not address whether that impact makes science an attractive commercial market.

r002.rationale: It says science progress may be driven by coding ability and writing and running programs, but does not clearly explain how AI-generated code lowers the barrier from a scientist’s idea to numerical testing.

r003.rationale: The response predicts progress in science but does not state that AI’s impact on basic research may come before a publicly attention-grabbing scientific breakthrough.

astra-6.text:
I think basic science is a very promising direction, but I would separate helping scientists do research from autonomously making scientific discoveries. The first can be useful much sooner. AI can help you read papers, write simulation code, analyze data, and explore possible explanations. The second requires a much longer loop: deciding which question matters, proposing a hypothesis, designing an experiment, and learning from the result.

Coding has a relatively convenient feedback loop. You can run a program, see an error, and try again. In science, getting feedback might require an experiment that takes weeks or expensive equipment. So the bottleneck may not be whether the model can produce an interesting idea, but whether it can test that idea and distinguish a real discovery from something that merely sounds plausible.

That makes me more optimistic initially about areas where experiments can be simulated or automated. There, you can build a loop in which the AI proposes something, gets reliable feedback, and improves. But even then, optimizing a measurable objective is different from choosing a new scientific question. I think AI can make substantial contributions before we solve that latter problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI’s promise in basic science but says nothing about commercial-market attractiveness.

r002.rationale: It says AI can help write simulation code, but does not state that AI-generated code lowers the practical barrier between a scientist’s idea and numerical testing.

r003.rationale: It says AI could contribute substantially before scientists can choose new questions, but does not connect that timing to a breakthrough attracting broad public attention.

sol-6.1.text:
I think basic science is a very promising direction, but I would distinguish between solving a well-defined scientific problem and doing research. If you have a clear objective and a reliable way to evaluate the answer, AI can make progress through a loop of proposing solutions, testing them, and learning from the results. Coding has that property: you can run the code and see what happens.

In science, the feedback loop is often much harder. An experiment might take weeks or months, and the result may be ambiguous. So the bottleneck may shift from the intelligence of the model to the speed and quality of experimentation. Areas where you can do useful simulations or automate experiments seem especially promising.

The other challenge is choosing the question. Producing a plausible hypothesis is different from identifying a question whose answer would change our understanding. I would look for systems that can carry a research project through that whole process: find an important uncertainty, design a useful experiment, interpret the evidence, and revise their approach. That would be a much stronger sign of a breakthrough than answering scientific questions well.

r001.rationale: The response calls basic science promising but says nothing about whether it is an attractive commercial market.

r002.rationale: It notes that code can be run and evaluated, but does not state that AI-generated code lowers the barrier for basic scientists to test ideas numerically.

r003.rationale: It discusses what would count as a research breakthrough, but does not say AI’s impact may come before a breakthrough that draws broad public attention.
